claim: 5-hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) accumulates at high levels in mammalian neurons.
source: It is present at approximately 10-fold higher levels in neurons than peripheral cell types (Globisch et al., 2010; Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Globisch et al., 2010; Kriaucionis and Heintz, 2009)

claim: 5hmC is produced from 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by the Ten-eleven translocation dioxygenases (Tet1, Tet2, Tet3).
source: 5-Hydroxymethylcytosine (5hmC) is produced from 5-methylcytosine (5mC) by the Ten-eleven translocation dioxygenases (Tet1, Tet2, Tet3) (Iyer et al., 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Iyer et al., 2009; Tahiliani et al., 2009)

claim: The distribution of 5hmC across the genome of adult neurons is cell specific and correlated with active gene expression.
source: its distribution across the genome of adult neurons is cell specific and correlated with active gene expression (Mellén et al., 2017; Mellén et al., 2012; Szulwach et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Mellén et al., 2017; Mellén et al., 2012; Szulwach et al., 2011)

claim: MeCP2 can bind probes containing 5hmC with high affinity.
source: The initial discovery that 5hmC accumulates within active gene bodies, coupled with the discovery that MeCP2 can bind probes containing 5hmC with high affinity, led to the proposal that MeCP2 binding within active genes facilitates their expression (Mellén et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Mellén et al., 2012)

claim: MeCP2 binds 5hmC at high affinity in non-CG dinucleotides but does not bind to 5hmCG.
source: Further studies demonstrating that MeCP2 binds 5hmC at high affinity in non-CG dinucleotides but does not bind to 5hmCG overturned this model (Ayata, 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Mellén et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Ayata, 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Mellén et al., 2017)

claim: Accumulation of 5hmCG and the depletion of 5hmCH in gene bodies is correlated with less MeCP2 binding and increased expression.
source: by revealing that accumulation of 5hmCG and the depletion of 5hmCH in gene bodies is correlated with less MeCP2 binding and increased expression (Ayata, 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Mellén et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Ayata, 2013; Gabel et al., 2015; Mellén et al., 2017)

claim: MeCP2 binding in living neurons is exquisitely sensitive to the levels of both 5mC and 5hmC.
source: Imaging of the binding and diffusion of single MeCP2 molecules in living neurons lacking Dnmt3a or Tet1, Tet2, and Tet3 demonstrate that its binding is exquisitely sensitive to the levels of both 5mC and 5hmC (Piccolo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Piccolo et al., 2019)

claim: Neuronal function is sensitive to MeCP2 gene dosage.
source: Given these data and the sensitivity of neuronal function to MeCP2 gene dosage (Chahrour et al., 2008; Nan and Bird, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chahrour et al., 2008; Nan and Bird, 2001)

claim: In dividing cells, 5hmC serves as an intermediate in DNA demethylation because maintenance DNA methyltransferases do not recognize hemi-hydroxymethylated cytosines.
source: In dividing cells, 5hmC serves as an intermediate in DNA demethylation because maintenance DNA methyltransferases do not recognize hemi-hydroxymethylated cytosines in order to reestablish methylation (Wu and Zhang, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Wu and Zhang, 2017)

claim: 5hmC is lost passively and replaced by C due to replicative dilution.
source: Consequently, 5hmC is lost passively and replaced by C due to replicative dilution.
evidence: Inferred from the mechanism described in the preceding sentence about maintenance methyltransferases not recognizing hemi-hydroxymethylated cytosines

claim: Loss of function studies in mouse embryonic stem cells have demonstrated that Tet-mediated replicative DNA demethylation provides full accessibility to regulatory regions necessary for expression of genes required for differentiation.
source: Loss of function studies in mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) (Dawlaty et al., 2013) and lymphocyte lineages Lio and Rao, 2019 have demonstrated that the role of Tet-mediated replicative DNA demethylation is to provide full accessibility to regulatory regions necessary for expression of genes required for differentiation.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Dawlaty et al., 2013; Lio and Rao, 2019)

claim: In B cells, Tet activity is required for demethylation and activation of enhancer regions that modulate AID expression to enable class switch recombination.
source: For example, at the activation-induced deaminase (AID) locus in B cells, Tet activity is required for demethylation and activation of enhancer regions that modulate AID expression to enable class switch recombination (Lio et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Lio et al., 2019)

claim: Tet-mediated replication-dependent passive demethylation is thought to be common in many dividing cell types, including progenitor cells in the developing nervous system.
source: Tet-mediated replication-dependent passive demethylation is thought to be common in many dividing cell types, including progenitor cells in the developing nervous system (MacArthur and Dawlaty, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (MacArthur and Dawlaty, 2021)

claim: Most neurons exit the cell cycle during mid-gestation and remain relatively simple and undifferentiated until birth.
source: Most neurons exit the cell cycle during mid-gestation and remain relatively simple and undifferentiated until birth.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about neuronal development

claim: Following parturition, neurons initiate an elaborate program of differentiation that includes dramatic increases in size, morphological complexity, and connectivity.
source: Following parturition, they initiate an elaborate program of differentiation that includes dramatic increases in size, morphological complexity, and connectivity.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about neuronal development

claim: 5hmC can be further oxidized by Tet proteins to produce 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC).
source: However, in addition to functional demethylation and passive demethylation, a third pathway for DNA demethylation, often referred to as active demethylation, has been proposed based on the finding that 5hmC can be further oxidized by Tet proteins to produce 5-formylcytosine (5fC) and 5-carboxylcytosine (5caC).
evidence: Statement of established biochemical pathway

claim: Removal of 5fC and 5caC by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG)-dependent base excision repair (BER) provides a mechanism for 5hmC-mediated DNA demethylation.
source: Removal of 5fC and 5caC by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG)-dependent base excision repair (BER) provides another mechanism for 5hmC-mediated DNA demethylation (He et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (He et al., 2011)

claim: Clear evidence that the TDG-BER pathway can operate in cultured cells has been presented.
source: Clear evidence that this pathway can operate in cultured cells has been presented, and detailed biochemical studies have delineated the mechanisms operating in TDG-BER DNA demethylation (Weber et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Weber et al., 2016)

claim: Active DNA demethylation is ideally suited for remodeling DNA methylation in postmitotic neurons.
source: Active DNA demethylation is ideally suited for remodeling DNA methylation in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: Logical inference based on the inability of postmitotic neurons to use replication-dependent demethylation

claim: Manipulations of Tet activity and 5hmC levels in cerebellar granule cell development provide strong evidence that 5hmC is required for expression of axon guidance and ion channel genes.
source: In studies of cerebellar granule cell development in ESC-derived GC cultures, primary GC cultures, and slice preparations, manipulations of Tet activity and 5hmC levels provide strong evidence that 5hmC is required for expression of axon guidance and ion channel genes, and that proper development of the GC dendritic arbor requires 5hmC (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Zhu et al., 2016)

claim: Proper development of the cerebellar granule cell dendritic arbor requires 5hmC.
source: In studies of cerebellar granule cell development in ESC-derived GC cultures, primary GC cultures, and slice preparations, manipulations of Tet activity and 5hmC levels provide strong evidence that 5hmC is required for expression of axon guidance and ion channel genes, and that proper development of the GC dendritic arbor requires 5hmC (Zhu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Zhu et al., 2016)

claim: Demethylation of 5hmC-GFP transfected DNA fragments retrieved after several days in culture display reduced 5hmC levels at several sites in HEK 293 cells and primary hippocampal neurons.
source: Demethylation of 5hmC-GFP transfected DNA fragments retrieved after several days in culture display reduced 5hmC levels at several sites as assessed by bisulfite sequencing (BSSeq) in HEK 293 cells and primary hippocampal neurons (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Guo et al., 2011)

claim: Changes in methylation levels at GGCC sites in the genome of hippocampal dentate gyrus neurons in response to electroconvulsive shock have been documented.
source: Changes in methylation levels at GGCC sites in the genome of hippocampal dentate gyrus neurons in response to electroconvulsive shock have been documented using the methylation-sensitive cut counting method that employs the methylation or hydroxymethylation-sensitive restriction enzyme HpaII and its methylation-insensitive isoschizomer Msp1 (Guo et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Guo et al., 2011)

claim: Global measurements of 5mC and 5hmC by mass spectroscopy in the hippocampus have shown that both decrease in response to the induction of seizure.
source: Global measurements of 5mC and 5hmC by mass spectroscopy in the hippocampus have shown that both decrease in response to the induction of seizure (Kaas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Kaas et al., 2013)

claim: In germline Tet1 knockout mice, Tet1 is required for proper regulation of the Npas4 and c-Fos promoters in both the cerebral cortex and hippocampus.
source: And in germline Tet1 knockout mice, analysis of the Npas4 and c-Fos promoters has shown that Tet1 is required for their proper regulation in both the cerebral cortex and hippocampus (Rudenko et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Rudenko et al., 2013)

claim: PC progenitors complete their final cell cycle between e10.5 and e13.5 within the ventricular zone of the developing cerebellar anlage.
source: In mice, PC progenitors complete their final cell cycle between e10.5 and e13.5 within the ventricular zone of the developing cerebellar anlage (Leto et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Leto et al., 2016)

claim: As PC progenitors exit cell cycle and commit to a PC fate, they express the transcription factors Lhx1/Lhx5.
source: As they exit cell cycle and commit to a PC fate, they express the transcription factors Lhx1/Lhx5 (Chizhikov et al., 2006; Morales and Hatten, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chizhikov et al., 2006; Morales and Hatten, 2006)

claim: The Pearson correlation coefficients between each replicate at all timepoints and techniques (RNASeq, OxBSSeq, ATACSeq, and ChIPSeq) were high (over 0.9).
source: The Pearson correlation coefficients between each replicate at all timepoints and techniques (RNASeq, OxBSSeq, ATACSeq, and ChIPSeq) were high (over 0.9), establishing that our data are reproducible and of very high quality (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-F

claim: Bisulfite conversion and oxidation rates for the OxBSSeq datasets were within the expected range.
source: Bisulfite conversion and oxidation rates for the OxBSSeq datasets were within the expected range (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G

claim: For the gene encoding the cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase (Prkg1), 5mCG is depleted and 5hmCG accumulates in the gene body as its expression increases between P0 and adult.
source: For example, in many genes, 5mCG is depleted and 5hmCG accumulates in the gene body as its expression increases between P0 and adult. This is clearly evident for the gene encoding the cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase (Prkg1), whose expression in PCs has been shown to be essential for long-term depression (Feil et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by data in the manuscript and citation to prior published work (Feil et al., 2003)

claim: Expression of Prkg1 in PCs is essential for long-term depression.
source: This is clearly evident for the gene encoding the cyclic GMP-dependent protein kinase (Prkg1), whose expression in PCs has been shown to be essential for long-term depression (Feil et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Feil et al., 2003)

claim: There is a global decrease of 5mCG and global increase of 5hmCG as PCs mature.
source: As these programs unfold, there is a global decrease of 5mCG and global increase of 5hmCG (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: There were 922 developmentally repressed genes (down-regulated in adult) enriched in categories involved in cell signaling and axon guidance pathways.
source: Using these criteria, there were 922 developmentally repressed genes (down-regulated in adult) enriched in categories involved in cell signaling and axon guidance pathways (e.g. Grid1, Pde1c; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and GO analysis shown in the manuscript

claim: 432 genes with increased expression as PCs differentiate encode proteins known to be important for the mature functions of PCs including calcium ion buffering and transport, regulation of the inositol triphosphate signaling pathway, and RNA splicing.
source: We identified 432 genes with increased expression as PCs differentiate encoding proteins known to be important for the mature functions of PCs including calcium ion buffering and transport, regulation of the inositol triphosphate signaling pathway, and RNA splicing.
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis and GO analysis shown in the manuscript

claim: Approximately half of the genes in the mouse genome are never expressed in PCs and remain heavily methylated and inaccessible.
source: Approximately half of the genes in the mouse genome (e.g. genes encoding olfactory receptors (Figure 1F), immunoglobulins, hemoglobin subunits, etc.) are never expressed in PCs and remain heavily methylated and inaccessible.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1F and analysis of epigenetic marks

claim: There is a second class of silent genes in PCs that are enriched in transcription factors expressed in very early embryos (Hox clusters, other homeobox genes, etc.) that are completely demethylated and enriched for the H3K27me3 histone mark.
source: As previously reported for other neurons (Mo et al., 2015), there is a second class of silent genes in PCs that are enriched in transcription factors expressed in very early embryos (Hox clusters, other homeobox genes, etc.). These are completely demethylated and enriched for the H3K27me3 histone mark, indicating that they are repressed by the polycomb repressive complex (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data in the manuscript and citations to prior published work (Mo et al., 2015; Li et al., 2018)

claim: Silent genes enriched in transcription factors expressed in very early embryos are repressed by the polycomb repressive complex.
source: These are completely demethylated and enriched for the H3K27me3 histone mark, indicating that they are repressed by the polycomb repressive complex (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by data in the manuscript and citation to prior published work (Li et al., 2018)

claim: Decreased expression during PC differentiation is associated with a loss of promoter accessibility as assayed by ATACSeq.
source: A consistent finding is that in most genes decreased expression is associated with a loss of promoter accessibility as assayed by assay for transposase-accessible chromatin sequencing (ATACSeq) (Figure 2D and K–L, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D, K-L, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Changes in promoter accessibility during PC differentiation are not correlated with changes in DNA methylation or H3K27me3 occupancy.
source: These changes are not correlated with changes in DNA methylation or H3K27me3 occupancy (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: 5hmCG accumulated over gene bodies early in development is stable or continues to increase during PC differentiation.
source: Furthermore, 5hmCG accumulated over the genes bodies early in development is stable or continues to increase (Figure 2C), suggesting that the presence of 5hmCG is not sufficient to maintain transcription.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: The presence of 5hmCG is not sufficient to maintain transcription.
source: Furthermore, 5hmCG accumulated over the genes bodies early in development is stable or continues to increase (Figure 2C), suggesting that the presence of 5hmCG is not sufficient to maintain transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that 5hmCG remains or increases in genes that become repressed

claim: There are at least two distinctly recognizable epigenetic patterns in genes that become repressed in PC development based on 5mCH and 5hmCH accumulation.
source: Interestingly, analysis of the repressive marks 5mCH and 5hmCH reveals at least two distinctly recognizable epigenetic patterns in genes that become repressed in PC development (Figure 2F–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G

claim: Repressed genes that accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH over their gene bodies are associated with lower promoter accessibility relative to those repressed genes with low levels of CH modification.
source: Repressed genes that accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH over their gene bodies (referred to as 'highCHmod' genes) are associated with lower promoter accessibility (Figure 2I) and enhanced accumulation (Figure 2H) of H3K27me3 relative to those repressed genes with low levels of CH modification (referred to as 'lowCHmod' genes) (Figure 2F–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G

claim: Repressed genes that accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH over their gene bodies show enhanced accumulation of H3K27me3 relative to those repressed genes with low levels of CH modification.
source: Repressed genes that accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH over their gene bodies (referred to as 'highCHmod' genes) are associated with lower promoter accessibility (Figure 2I) and enhanced accumulation (Figure 2H) of H3K27me3 relative to those repressed genes with low levels of CH modification (referred to as 'lowCHmod' genes) (Figure 2F–J, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2F-J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F-G

claim: Both sets of genes that are repressed as PC differentiation proceeds are associated with development.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis indicates that both sets of genes that are repressed as PC differentiation proceeds are associated with development, and that the genes that do not accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH encode preferentially proteins related to cell morphogenesis and axonal projection (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2J

claim: Genes that do not accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH during repression encode preferentially proteins related to cell morphogenesis and axonal projection.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis indicates that both sets of genes that are repressed as PC differentiation proceeds are associated with development, and that the genes that do not accumulate 5mCH and 5hmCH encode preferentially proteins related to cell morphogenesis and axonal projection (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2J

claim: The data for highCHmod genes is consistent with transcriptional inhibition through both polycomb repressive complexes and MeCP2 binding.
source: Although the data for highCHmod genes is consistent with transcriptional inhibition through both polycomb repressive complexes (Li et al., 2018) and MeCP2 binding (Gabel et al., 2015), our data do not identify the mechanisms responsible for repression of the lowCHmod gene class that fail to accumulate repressive CH marks over the gene body as they mature.
evidence: Inferred from the epigenetic marks observed and citations to prior published work (Li et al., 2018; Gabel et al., 2015)

claim: The mechanisms responsible for repression of the lowCHmod gene class are not identified by the data.
source: Although the data for highCHmod genes is consistent with transcriptional inhibition through both polycomb repressive complexes (Li et al., 2018) and MeCP2 binding (Gabel et al., 2015), our data do not identify the mechanisms responsible for repression of the lowCHmod gene class that fail to accumulate repressive CH marks over the gene body as they mature.
evidence: Explicit statement that the data do not identify the mechanisms

claim: 432 genes increase in expression as PCs differentiate.
source: We identified 432 genes that increase in expression as PCs differentiate (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 1

claim: Genes that increase in expression as PCs differentiate encode proteins known to be important for the mature functions of PCs, including calcium ion buffering and transport, regulation of the inositol triphosphate signaling pathway, and RNA splicing.
source: In general, these genes encode proteins known to be important for the mature functions of PCs, including calcium ion buffering and transport, regulation of the inositol triphosphate signaling pathway, and RNA splicing (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: The chromatin landscape of most genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation is similar to those that are constitutively transcribed.
source: The chromatin landscape of most genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation is similar to those that are constitutively transcribed (e.g. Atp2a3, Cep76; Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1G

claim: Genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation have promoters that are highly accessible.
source: Their promoters are highly accessible (Figure 2D and K–L)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and K-L

claim: Genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation have high levels of H3K4me3.
source: they have high levels of H3K4me3 (Figure 2E)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation have gene bodies with low levels of 5mCG and elevated levels of 5hmCG.
source: their gene bodies have low levels of 5mCG and elevated levels of 5hmCG (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Genes whose expression increases during PC differentiation do not accumulate 5mCH or 5hmCH.
source: and they do not accumulate 5mCH or 5hmCH (Figure 2N).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2N

claim: In a small subset of highly expressed genes (e.g. Cep76, Itpr1, Mtss1) there is a profound loss of both 5hmCG and 5mCG during the terminal, postmitotic stage of PC differentiation.
source: Thus, in a small subset of highly expressed genes (e.g. Cep76, Itpr1, Mtss1) there is a profound loss of both 5hmCG and 5mCG during the terminal, postmitotic stage of PC differentiation (Figures 1F and 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 1F and 3

claim: Multiple DNA methylation valleys (DMVs) longer than 15 kb were identified in PCs.
source: This revealed multiple regions longer than 15 kb, an unusual finding given that the average length of DMVs is ~5 kb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E; Jeong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E and citation to prior published work (Jeong et al., 2014)

claim: The average length of DMVs is ~5 kb.
source: This revealed multiple regions longer than 15 kb, an unusual finding given that the average length of DMVs is ~5 kb (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E; Jeong et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Jeong et al., 2014)

claim: A small number of DMV-containing genes are inactive, fully demethylated, inaccessible, and covered by high levels of H3K27me3 repressive marks.
source: As expected from previous studies, a small number of these genes are inactive, fully demethylated, inaccessible, and covered by high levels of H3K27me3 repressive marks (Figure 3A, Foxd1, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C

claim: Inactive DMV-containing genes acquire their characteristics early in development, and their epigenetic features are stable.
source: These genes acquire their characteristics early in development, and their epigenetic features are stable.
evidence: Supported by data shown in the manuscript

claim: The majority of very large DMVs in PCs arise during differentiation through loss of 5mC and 5hmC over active, highly expressed genes as PCs mature.
source: The majority of very large DMVs in PCs, however, arise during differentiation through loss of 5mC and 5hmC over active, highly expressed genes as PCs mature (Figure 3, Itpr1, Mtss1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3

claim: At birth, genes that develop large DMVs are actively transcribed, 5hmCG is enriched in the gene body and 5mCG is depleted, their promoters are accessible, and H3K4me3 is present over their promoters.
source: At birth, these genes are actively transcribed (Figure 3A), 5hmCG is enriched in the gene body (Figure 3B) and 5mCG is depleted (Figure 3C), their promoters are accessible (Figure 3D), and H3K4me3 is present over their promoters (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A-E

claim: As differentiation proceeds and transcription increases in genes that develop large DMVs, there is a gradual decrease in both 5mCG, 5hmCG, and H3K27me3 histone marks, and ATAC accessibility and H4K4me3 marks spread from the promoter into the gene body.
source: As differentiation proceeds and transcription increases, there is a gradual decrease in both 5mCG, 5hmCG, and H3K27me3 histone marks, and ATAC accessibility and H4K4me3 marks spread from the promoter into the gene body.
evidence: Supported by data shown in the manuscript

claim: Hypo-DMRs present at P0 expand and fuse as PCs lose both methylation and hydroxymethylation to form the very large DMRs that are characteristics of these genes.
source: These data also reveal that hypo-DMRs (differentially methylated regions) present at P0 expand and fuse as PCs lose both methylation and hydroxymethylation to form the very large DMRs that are characteristics of these genes (Figure 3A, hypo-DMR track).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Loss of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation occurs over the entire gene body for genes that develop large DMVs as H3K4me3 activating histone marks accumulate and ATAC accessibility increases.
source: As shown in Figure 3B–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-K, quantitation of these features demonstrates that that loss of DNA methylation and hydroxymethylation occurs over the entire gene body for these genes as H3K4me3 activating histone marks accumulate and ATAC accessibility increases.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B-E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I-K

claim: Many of the active genes associated with broad DMVs are PC-specific and highly expressed.
source: Interestingly, many of the active genes associated with broad DMVs are PC-specific and highly expressed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Active genes associated with broad DMVs are involved in the inositol triphosphate/calcium signaling pathways, and a subset is associated with ataxia and autism.
source: GO analysis indicates that they are involved in the inositol triphosphate/calcium signaling pathways, and a subset is associated with ataxia and autism (Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1H

claim: Active genes associated with broad DMVs do not accumulate modified cytosines in CpH context.
source: They do not accumulate modified cytosines in CpH context (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G

claim: DNA demethylation can occur in postmitotic neurons.
source: These data provide strong evidence that DNA demethylation can occur in postmitotic neurons, and that it is enhanced in a specific class of genes that are very highly expressed and functionally important.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of 5mC and 5hmC in postmitotic PCs

claim: DNA demethylation is enhanced in a specific class of genes that are very highly expressed and functionally important.
source: These data provide strong evidence that DNA demethylation can occur in postmitotic neurons, and that it is enhanced in a specific class of genes that are very highly expressed and functionally important.
evidence: Supported by data showing loss of 5mC and 5hmC in highly expressed genes with large DMVs

claim: Mass spectroscopic analysis of genomic DNA from differentiating PCs failed to detect 5fC or 5caC.
source: Although our mass spectroscopic analysis of genomic DNA from differentiating PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L) failed to detect 5fC or 5caC, their involvement as transient intermediates in the loss of 5mC and 5hmC cannot be ruled out because the small fraction of the genome covered by this gene class may preclude their detection (Guo et al., 2011; He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L

claim: The involvement of 5fC and 5caC as transient intermediates in the loss of 5mC and 5hmC cannot be ruled out because the small fraction of the genome covered by this gene class may preclude their detection.
source: Although our mass spectroscopic analysis of genomic DNA from differentiating PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L) failed to detect 5fC or 5caC, their involvement as transient intermediates in the loss of 5mC and 5hmC cannot be ruled out because the small fraction of the genome covered by this gene class may preclude their detection (Guo et al., 2011; He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011).
evidence: Logical inference based on the small fraction of the genome undergoing demethylation and citations to prior published work (Guo et al., 2011; He et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2011)

claim: Activation of enhancers and other regulatory sites is accompanied by increased ATAC accessibility and loss of DNA methylation.
source: Previous studies of enhancers and other regulatory sites have established that their activation is accompanied by increased ATAC accessibility and loss of DNA methylation (Lio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Lio et al., 2016)

claim: ATAC peaks that gain accessibility lose both 5hmC and 5mC as cells progress from P0 to adult.
source: As anticipated, those ATAC peaks that gain accessibility lose both 5hmC and 5mC as cells progress from P0 to adult (Figure 2N, Gain section)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2N

claim: No significant changes in methylation at ATAC peak centers occur in sites that lose accessibility.
source: whereas no significant changes in methylation at ATAC peak centers occur in sites that lose accessibility (Figure 2N, Loss section).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2N

claim: The transcription factor motifs found in different classes of ATAC sites are distinct.
source: Although these ATAC peaks have not been identified as active enhancers, it is noteworthy that the transcription factor motifs found in these different classes of ATAC sites are distinct (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: Enhancer activation is accompanied by enhanced ATAC accessibility and DNA demethylation.
source: These findings are consistent with prior studies indicating that enhancer activation is accompanied by enhanced ATAC accessibility and DNA demethylation (Lio et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by data in the manuscript and citation to prior published work (Lio et al., 2016)

claim: DNA demethylation in ATAC accessible sites does not require cell division.
source: In this case, however, DNA demethylation does not require cell division.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that demethylation occurs in postmitotic PCs

claim: The onset of expression of the Pcp2 gene and the corresponding BAC vector occurs approximately 1 week after birth as the cerebellum enters its terminal phase of development and maturation.
source: We chose to drive Cre recombinase expression using an engineered Pcp2 BAC employed previously to generate accurate Cre driver lines (Gong et al., 2007) because the onset of expression of the Pcp2 gene and the corresponding BAC vector occurs approximately 1 week after birth as the cerebellum enters its terminal phase of development and maturation.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Gong et al., 2007)

claim: PCR analysis of the floxed regions of each Tet gene in purified PC genomic DNA confirmed the deletion of exons from all three TET proteins.
source: PCR analysis of the floxed regions of each Tet gene in purified PC genomic DNA, and RNASeq analysis confirmed the deletion of exons from all three TET proteins (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D

claim: The Pcp2TetTKO lines displayed no gross motor phenotype as assessed by rotarod performance.
